title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
hook: out of the sun, into the shade, and back out again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's elephant: a reaching trunk, steadied by a chain to hold, a name or the breath. What did you give your attention to hold? Your line was give the trunk a chain. Day nine hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.

Midday, a hot road, no wind. A traveler steps under a tree and the relief is instant. A few minutes later, something across the road catches the eye, and the traveler walks back out into the glare to get it. Then back to the shade. Then out again. Ramana Maharshi draws that scene in Who Am I?, near the end, and he uses it to answer the question the text opened with: where is happiness?
screen: `A HOT ROAD AT MIDDAY.` → `INTO THE SHADE, AND OUT AGAIN.` → `WHERE IS HAPPINESS?`

segments.voice: Remember how the text began: everyone wants to be happy. Here, Ramana says where that happiness is. Not in things, he says. When we get something we wanted, we feel happy, and we credit the thing. But what really happened, in his account, is that the wanting stopped for a moment. The mind went quiet and turned back toward the self, and the happiness we felt was the self's own. Then the next want shows up, and we walk back into the sun. The one who knows this, he says, stays in the shade. Then, close by, a line for anyone who feels too far gone for any of this. Even someone who has done great wrong, Ramana says, shouldn't sit weeping, I'm a sinner, how can I be saved? Drop the thought I'm a sinner, he says, and get on with the inquiry. In his account, the heavy story about yourself is one more thought, and it gets the same question as the rest. Now look back at this week. It opened with Vivekananda's Raja Yoga: a lab where the mind is the instrument. A monkey, wild with wine and a sting, and the first lesson: watch it jump. A lake: still the waves and the bottom shows. Then Ramana. Who am I?, with body, senses and mind set aside. To whom did this thought come?, and the stick that burns at the end. An elephant given a chain. And today, the shade. Two teachers, two languages of practice, and in both their accounts one claim underneath: what the seeker is looking for was there before the looking started. Tomorrow, a different kind of teacher: Aurobindo.
screen: `HAPPINESS IS NOT IN THINGS.` · `THE WISE ONE STAYS IN THE SHADE.` · `DROP THE THOUGHT 'I'M A SINNER.'` · then, large: `THE WEEK: A MONKEY, A LAKE, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Recall one small happiness from this week: a meal, a message, a moment of quiet. Notice how, just then, the wanting paused. Now see if you can find that pause again, without the thing. Rest in the shade for a while. When a want pulls you back out into the sun, notice it, and ask whose want it is. If a heavy thought about yourself arrives, give it the same question. If you pray, you can let the resting be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said happiness isn't in things but in the self, and that the wise one stays in the shade.
Your line: stays in the shade. Today, the next time you get something you wanted, notice the quiet that comes just after, and stay in the shade a moment longer. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Who Am I? return to it as a daily text; at Ramana's ashram in Tiruvannamalai, visitors sit in silence in the hall where he lived and walk around the hill of Arunachala.

original.note: Tamil, in Tamil script: Nan Yar, 'who am I?', the name of Ramana's text in the language he wrote it in.

trapdoor: what you thought: happiness is in getting what you want.
what it means: Ramana says getting it only quiets the wanting for a moment, and the happiness was the self's all along.
what a scholar hears: the shade and the sun, near the end of Nan Yar, answering the text's opening line that every being wants to be happy.
